Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): On behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I desire to move, seconded by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe):
That Mr. William Henry Golding be appointed as deputy chairman of committees of the whole house.
[Mr. Chevrier.l
The essential reason for this motion is one of procedure. If the records of 1938 are referred to, all the precedents will be found. Section 3 of the Speaker of the House of Commons Act provides that whenever the house is informed by the Clerk at the table of the unavoidable absence of the Speaker, the chairman of committees shall take the chair and exercise the authority of the Speaker for twenty-four hours. It follows from this that the Speaker only, or the Deputy Speaker if the Speaker is unavoidably absent, can open the sittings of the house. If they were both absent at three o'clock the sittings of the house could not be opened.
In order to avoid such an occurrence the house added in 1939 the following provision as section 5 of standing order 56:
At the commencement of every session, or from time to time as necessity may arise, the house may appoint a deputy chairman of committees who shall, whenever the chairman of committees is absent, he entitled to exercise all the powers vested in the chairman of committees including his powers as Deputy Speaker during Mr. Speaker's unavoidable absence.
After this new standing order was passed the leader of the house moved that a certain hon. gentleman be appointed. I understand that Your Honour has consulted with the leaders of the various parties and groups in the house.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I am delighted that this motion has been sponsored by the right hon. gentleman. On two occasions I had the honour of visiting the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding) and his constituents. Fie is one of the worthiest members of the House of Commons. He is a wise man; he is a good Liberal; he is a true Liberal; he is broadminded; he is devoted to his duty; he has judgment and tact; he has determination. He acquired these attributes because of his long experience in the municipal life of his community, first as councillor and then as alderman. I am delighted that the merits of the hon. gentleman are being recognized. He is the chairman of the Liberal caucus-*

speechtext: The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time that we have had occasion to refer to the electoral methods used in the constituency of Montreal-Cartier. There was an election in 1943 and another one in 1945. Previous to the 1943 and 1945 elections there had been a provincial election where Mr. Cohen had been elected. In some polls when the box was opened at six o'clock it was found that although the list contained only 100 or 150 names, more than 200 voters had registered. In 1943 the electoral lists were prepared by the enumerators. At that time hundreds of people were disfranchised1. The same thing happened in 1945. Now we see a repetition of what took place in 1943 and 1945. The only difference is that it has been aggravated. In 1943 and 1945 the names of hundreds of people were omitted from the list. This time not only were names omitted from the list, but after receiving certificates stating that their names would be inscribed on the electoral lists, people received notices that because of affidavits made by unknown people, affidavits not sworn and in some cases not even signed, their names were to be removed.
What took place? Let me give just one example. In one poll in Montreal there is a man who is well known all over the province. I refer to Doctor Stephen Langevin, who has been living on Sherbrooke street for the last thirty years. He is a property owner. He was 
visited one day by the enumerators who, mind you, were appointed at the suggestion of the two candidates, communist and Liberal. He received a certificate stating that his name would be inscribed on the list. A few days later he received notice stating that his name would be omitted because he had moved. He is there; he is a property owner. He has never lived anywhere but in that block; he has been practising there all the time. On the last day or second last day he went to the office of the revising officer because he wanted his name on the list. Several hundred people were waiting to get into that office. He could not get in, but while he was waiting he made up a list of I do not know how many names of people who were also waiting because they had received similar notices. They were waiting, but they could not get in either. Now this gentleman and all his family will lose their votes on March 31; and that is just one example.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the primary right of a man in a democratic country is the right to register his vote when an election is held to return a representative to the House of Commons. In this election some 1,500 people in Montreal will be deprived of that right on March 31 because of these irregularities. I hold the government responsible for this because these officers are employed and paid by the government, with the money of the public.
In this instance three persons, Paul Rioux, Charles Frechette, and Roland Beaudoin alias Beaudin, swore to affidavits that Doctor Langevin and others had moved or were unknown. I have a list here of the names of some of the people:	Anna St. Vincent,
Madame E. Parent, Madame E. Brisebois, Mademoiselle Florida Gagnon, Madame Ernest Parent, Omer Gagne, Samuel Brisebois, Madame Eugenie Alarie, Madame J. Roch, Monsieur J. Roch, Mr. N. O. Laeelle, Madame O. Laeelle, Monsieur A. Arsenault, Miss M. Provost, Mr. Roland Guay, Madame Jacqueline Alteben, Mademoiselle Cordelia Gagnon, Madame Pineault, Mademoiselle Clarice Langevin, Mademoiselle Antoinette Dionne.
These are a few of the names of the people who are going to be deprived of their right to vote on Monday next. Other persons have been struck off the list because of declarations which do not contain any reason why this should be done. According to electoral law such affidavits must set out the cause for which it is asked that these people be struck off the list.

Cartier By-Election
It has been, said that there was no recourse, no remedy for this situation. There was one, a very clear remedy. I quote section 99 of the Dominion Elections Act:
If during the course of any election it transpires that insufficient time has been allowed or insufficient election officers or polling stations have been provided for the execution of any of the purposes of this act, by reason of the operation of any provision of this act or of any mistake or miscalculation or of any unforeseen emergency, the chief electoral officer may, notwithstanding anything in this act, extend the time for doing any act or acts, increase the number of election officers, including revising officers, who shall however, be appointed by the appropriate ex-officio revising officer, who has been appointed for the performance of any duty, or increase the number of polling stations-
The chief electoral officer had the right to increase the number of revising officers when hundreds of persons were waiting at the office to answer these false affidavits. The door was *closed at ten o'clock, however, and they were given no hearing. This was known by everybody, because these facts were published in the newspapers. The chief electoral officer knew about it; he was called here but he did not want to do anything, and there the matter stands.
I said some people have been struck off the list at the instance of people who have not even sworn to the notice they have handed the revising officer. In this connection I could quote many names. I have here a *copy of the notice served on an elector. What happened? The elector received a notice that somebody had sworn in an affidavit that he *was unknown, or that he had moved. This notice was delivered by registered mail. Who delivered that registered letter! It was delivered by employees of the post office department. They knew these people were there, because the letter was delivered, but in spite of that fact no one said anything and the government did nothing. More than that, the names of electors which already had been inscribed by the enumerators were struck out even before affidavits were given the revising officers. I have the proof here. Some notices were sent under date of March 14, while the affidavits were not signed until March 15.
I do not want to delay the business of the -committee more than is necessary, but this is an important matter. I think I have said enough to convince the people that although we .are supposed to live in a democratic country, we are not in fact living in a democratic country'. As I said, the primary right of anyone living in a democratic country is the right to register his vote when an election is held to -.elect representatives to the House of Commons.
At the present time we are complaining that the people have no more confidence in public men, but what confidence can you have when you see all these things going on, I would not say with their consent but at least with their benevolent knowledge?
An lion. MEMBER: Blessing.

"Blessing", somebody said. They say that they are fighting communism, but if the Liberal candidate in Cartier is fighting communism he and his representatives are adopting the communist method. There is no difference between what is going on in Cartier during this election and what has gone on in Russia or Poland.
I thank you. Mr. Chairman, for having allowed me to give a few facts. Before concluding my remarks may I say that I think there is still time for the government to act. The election is going to take place on Monday-
Postpone it.
No; the election is going to take place on Monday. The chief electoral officer could appoint some revising officers, or he could increase the number of officers to receive these complaints.
That is the law.
The law is there; the law is clear. Section 99 gives the chief electoral officer the power to extend the time for anything which is included in the act.
Was that asked for?
It was.
By whom?
I called up personally. I did not speak to the chief electoral officer, but I spoke to his son *who is in the office and he told me that he could not do anything.
That is hearsay evidence.

I am told that they called his attention to that. Even if his attention was not called to it, these things are known all over the country. People know what is going on in Cartier at the present time. I appeal to the government to be fair and to do what they can do before March 31.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Mr. Chairman, I have listened with much interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie. I am sure that everybody in this committee agrees that there is nothing that should be conserved as a more precious privilege than the right, of those who are entitled to do so, to vote. Parliament has provided an elections act which I think in a general way contains all the safeguards which members of parliament felt could be devised to assure that individuals might properly exercise that right. The act provides for the office of chief electoral officer. From the knowledge I have had of what has been going on I am. sure that everyone has confidence in our chief electoral officer. I think everyone feels that he endeavours to administer that act in a fair, impartial and judicious way and to carry it out in the spirit in which it was passed.
Parliament has provided that enumerators shall be appointed. These enumerators are appointed by the returning * officer, but I understand that they are designated by the representatives of the two parties who obtained the largest number of votes at the preceding election. There is possibly a weakness in the act with respect to the remuneration of enumerators at the rate of so much per name. I do not think that is the best way in which the remuneration of enumerators should be provided for. It may prove to be an incentive to gather as many names as possible for which they are paid, I think at the rate of seven cents per name, as part of the election expense.
However that may be, the act provides that the chief justice shall be ex-officio the revising officer and that he shall appoint his assistants. That is what was done in Cartier. I am sure that all those who have the privilege of knowing Chief Justice O. S. Tyndale will be confident that he would not be a party to nor would he tolerate anything that might amount to interference with the exercise of an elector's franchise. Presumably the chief justice appointed revising officers. The act provides that when the lists are drawn up the electors in the constituency may object to names. The hon. member says that objections were filed to some 1,500 names and that in accordance with the terms of the act they were stricken from the list. Notice was given to those whose names had thus been objected to.
The hon. member says that the revising officers closed the offices at ten o'clock at night before an opportunity had been given to all those who had responded to the notices to state their cases. I do not know about that personally. I do know that there were complaints of offices having been closed and that application was made to the courts in

that regard. That is not something with which the government has to do. It is not something that it would be tolerable to have a government deal with; it must be something under the control of the judicial authority.
The revision was performed under the control of the judicial authority. Application was made to the courts alleging that there had been irregularities. I have not the record before me, but the newspapers report that application was made to the courts and that the justice who disposed of the application was one who formerly occupied the chair of this house. I think he is known to a large number of the members of the house. He heard the application, he considered the facts which the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie has mentioned, and he dismissed the application, saying that there was nothing under the act which he could do or order.
The hon. member says that there is something that could be done by the chief electoral officer. I should be glad if he would suggest what could be done by the chief electoral officer.

There is section 99.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Is that the section which says that the chief electoral officer can extend delays? What is the suggestion of the hon. member? Does he suggest that the chief electoral officer should postpone the date of the election? I should be glad if the hon. member would make a concrete suggestion, because I am sure there is not a single member in this house who would not concur in the adoption of any practical suggestion that might be made. It may be that our law, in spite of our best efforts-when I say "our best efforts" I mean the best efforts of the members of parliament-to make it a good law, is deficient in some respect. If it is and there results any kind of prejudice there could be a contestation and an invalidation of the election. If the hon. gentleman feels that there is anything at this time that can be suggested to the chief electoral officer that would take care of what he says are grievances I would be glad if he would make the suggestions and I am sure that, if they are practicable, there is not a member of this house who would not applaud his suggestions and recommend, so far as the members of this house have authority to do so to the chief electoral officer, that he implement them.
I am sure that no one wants to see a single elector deprived of the right to cast his vote. I have been told that there are some 37;000 names on this list. It is unfortunately one of

the consequences of the greater congestion of population that we know less about each other. The closer we live together in large cities, the less we know about our immediate neighbours, and it is quite possible that affidavits may have been filed by people who said So-and-so is unknown. I am sure that there are people living probably within one hundred yards of me in Ottawa who are unknown to me. That is one of the unfortunate circumstances which arise in congested districts. In the rural districts we all know each other. It may very well be that there is a deficiency in the act. It may very well be that it should not be possible to strike a name off a prepared list on the simple affidavit of some other elector that that name is unknown. That operates satisfactorily in rural parts, but I am not at all convinced that it should be possible to strike a name off a list in a congested area merely because some elector comes along and says, "That name is unknown to me".

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not trying to defend anything. I am merely saying that in that congested area it is quite conceivable that
1.500	names would be unknown to a very large number of those residing in that constituency. But that is something that does not take care of the present grievance. Mr. Chairman, I was very glad to hear the right hon. minister say that this house under noi circumstances either directly or indirectly would approve any procedure which would deprive any elector of his right to vote. After all, that is one of the sacred rights which are left to us, the right to vote.
I listened carefully to what the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie said. I for one consider him to be a gentleman and a man of great experience who would certainly not come before the house at this time and delay its ordinary business just for the sake of putting before the house something he could not substantiate. That is the problem with which they are faced.
I am not prepared to say that this house can solve that problem today; I agree with the minister there, except possibly that the documents which my hon. friend has could be submitted immediately to the chief electoral officer. If the chief electoral officer is satisfied that there has been disfranchisement, whether in good faith or in bad faith, revising officers could be appointed today and ordered to sit tomorrow and Sunday and hear these
1,500	cases and find out whether they have been disfranchised rightly or wrongly. I have not scrutinized the act but certainly justice should be done. We are faced with affidavits and charges that fellow Canadians have been disfranchised. I have before me two of these affidavits which have been handed to me by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie and which tell the story. I am sure that no hon. member with legal training would be able to explain why these documents were prepared in this way. It is known that ways and means are provided in the electoral act of denouncing, if I may use that word, to the electoral officer an elector whose name should be struck off the list. There are forms provided by the chief electoral officer in which the denouncing person can insert the name of a person who, he thinks, should be disfranchised, and giving the reason therefor. This particular notice was sent to Mr. Gagne Omer, 270 Deboisbriand, Montreal, who is the elector threatened with disfranchisement. I am not trying to allege anything I cannot prove.

The other notice was sent to Mr. Jean-Paul Coctu-I shall not attempt to analyse the name-residing at 4381 St. Dominique, Montreal, and was signed by the revising officer on the 14th day of March, 1947. Mr. ST. LAURENT: It would appear from the documents which the hon. member sent me that there is something irregular there. I am not going to take any part in the argument now before the committee. No one can condone striking names off the list, if they should be on. I merely rose to explain how names are put on the list. According to the act at the present time in a city subdivision two enumerators go together to call on householders and ask for the names in a house. Unquestionably enumerators have not always done what they should. I have known enumerators to say to each other, ''You take that side of the street and I shall take the other." In that way irregularities creep in. Of course they get through the subdivision much quicker. They get seven cents a name, and they earn their seven cents much more rapidly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I should like hon. members to keep order. It is most difficult for the hon. member who is trying to speak; I can hardly follow him.

I am sure that the committee which has been appointed to make some revision in the election act will take into consideration what has been said by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie. The chief electoral officer himself, who is thoroughly qualified and eminently honourable, will be of great assistance in assisting the committee to make the changes that should be made. It is a serious offence to strike names off the list. On the other hand, it is the simplest thing in the world to put names on. It is no trick at all to put names on which should not be there, because the enumerators are paid seven cents a name. They are not compelled to make certain that the names which they are writing down are names of people who actually reside in the house or in the apartment. They put the name down. Every hon. member, particularly those representing city ridings, know of many names which have been put on the lists and which should not be put there. On the other hand, there is no defence for striking off names that should be on the list.
The suggestion made by the hon. member for Argenteuil is a good one if it can be carried out. Certainly the house should see to it-if it is at all possible to do it, and surely it is not too late to do it-that every man and woman entitled to vote in the riding of Montreal-Cartier should be given the privilege of voting.

That there is opportunity for discussing and improving the election act goes without saying, but really that is not

Interim Supply
the matter that is before us. The question is, can we do anything to ensure an honest and fair election in the riding which is voting on Monday next? I have not the election act before me. I have taken a hurried look at the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, and if the power to correct this hateful situation is not found in that act, it is the only power that is missing therefrom. speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: To the best of my knowledge no agreement has been entered into as yet with the government of Peru. Negotiations are taking place. The proposal is with regard to the fourth freedom. There will be mutual exchange under the fourth freedom and the Peruvian airways will have the right to land in Canada and deliver passengers from Pern destined for Canada and to pick up in Canada passengers destined for Peru. Is it intended that airways between Peru and Canada will be operated by the Peruvian government or by a company organized under the laws of Peru?

speechtext: It is a company organized under the laws of Peru. The question of ownership has been examined both by the United States and by Canada and we are satisfied that the position of ownership complies with the Canadian regulations.

During and since the war, the Canadian wheat board has been engaged in a number of operations in grain and seeds under the authority of various orders in council under the War Measures Act and the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. I should perhaps add, so that there may be no misunderstanding, that these deficits have nothing to do with the wheat board's ordinary business of buying and selling farmers' wheat. They arose out of emergency operations which have already come to an end.

You were very naive.

But again it is impossible for the Speaker to provide better accommodation for these girls because we simply have not the accommodation. Hon. members may know that during last session it happened about a dozen times that a committee was supposed to meet and the chairmen of different committees standing around in the corridors of this House of Commons came to the Speaker to find accommodation because all the regular committee rooms were taken. So I would take this opportunity to call the attention of the minister concerned to the situation to see if it would not be possible to provide more accommodation for the need of members of the house.

May I ask the Speaker, before he sits down, a question having to do with another matter? Has any consideration been given by the Speaker or by the government to changing the hours of sitting of the House of Commons? I have a suggestion to make which is strictly personal and informal, since I have not discussed it with anybody except in an informal way. But I think consideration might be given to the House of Commons relegating its old tradition of sitting from three o'clock in the afternoon until eleven o'clock at night. The difficulties of the * staff of the house have been mentioned and no one has more sympathy with them than I have, but I think our own position should also be carefully studied. I suggest that we should sit from one o'clock to seven o'clock and then call it a day. In that way we would gain three hours on Wednesday. While my suggestion is purely a personal one, I think it would meet with a good deal of approval from the members generally and it would allow us to live more normal lives in this city. We cannot live an absolutely normal life as members of parliament, but it does seem to me that it is hardly fair to ask anybody to work until eleven o'clock at night, no matter how young or how old he may be.

The explanation for the additional amount required is as follows: due to expanded mining activities in the Yellowknife mining district and administrative responsibilties in the Mackenzie district as a whole, it is necessary to provide increased living and office accommodation, also additional quarters and guardroom for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The construction of buildings was commenced in 1946 but difficulties in purchasing materials and transporting them to various posts prevented the buildings being completed in 1946.
In 1945, the sum of $140,000 was allocated from the war appropriation and subsequently voted as a supplementary estimate for the government of the northwest territories. These funds were made available to the Department of Public Works for dismantling American buildings and salvaging materials for the construction of new buildings. A considerable amount of materials, including over 1,000,000 f.b.m. lumber was salvaged from these buildings at Waterways, Alberta, and Fort Smith, northwest territories. The dismantling of these American buildings was continued in 1946. The sum of $375,700 was provided in the 1946-47 estimates for the construction of departmental buildings.
Supply-National Revenue

In 1946-47, the Department of Public Works carried the following building programme for this department:
(a)	continuation of the dismantling of buildings at Waterways and Fort Smith. The materials salvaged were bundled, labelled and shipped to Fort Smith, Yellowknife and other settlements for building purposes.
(b)	construction of administration building, three residences, and garage at Fort Smith.
(c)	construction of administration building, two double duplex apartment buildings and a new liquor store building at Yellowknife. The erection of several Dallas huts and igloos for living quarters and storage of materials at Yellowknife. The construction of wardens' houses and erection of prefabricated warehouses at Fort Resolution, Fort Simpson and Fort Norman. These buildings, although occupied, are not completely finished.
(d)	shipment of building materials to Akla-vik for the construction of a warden's residence next summer.
(e)	distribution of building materials to the Wood Buffalo Park for use by the park wardens in the construction of new dwellings.
The Department of Public Works, which is in charge of actual construction, has reported that this further amount is required to take care of obligations incurred during 1946-47. The cost of building in the Mackenzie district has been much greater than anyone anticipated, but it was necessary to proceed with the programme to house essential departmental activities due to rapidly increasing developments.

I have a question to ask on this item which has to do with taxation. Farmers in western Canada who delivered grain in 1944 find that they are now taxed on

the grain which they delivered in that year, which has increased their income to the point where they become taxable, some of them rather heavily. The grain which they delivered in 1944 was grown in 1942 and 1943. Under the government quota system and regulations, they were not permitted to deliver grain at that time. When they delivered grain in 1944 it put them in an income tax bracket. Because of their desire to help win the war in 1944 and because they held back their grain in 1942 and 1943 they are being heavily penalized. There is an injustice there which the minister should look into and try to rectify. I do not find these people objecting to paying taxes when there is income taxable in a particular year, but when they are compelled to pay income tax on income earned on work which they did in 1942 and 1943 it is discrimination. Farmers in other parts of the community and other taxpayers in Canada are not taxed in 1944 on income earned in 1942 and 1943. What is happening is that the whole thing is lumped together in 1944 and tax is assessed on it. These people are being taxed on grain grown in 1942 and 1943 which was not marketed, nor did they receive any money for it until 1944. They were not allowed to deliver the grain which they had. Had they been allowed to deliver the grain, they would not have been taxable because they did not have taxable income. Government regulations prohibited them from getting money for their work in those years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no space in which to put the grain.

That is right. They had to go to the extra expense of storing that grain on the farms and building granaries. Government regulations prevented them from delivering the grain. As a result, income rightly belonging to 1942 and 1943 was lumped together and put in 1944. It would be equivalent to members of parliament not being able to get their income for 1942 and 1943; then having the whole thing lumped together in 1944 and being charged income tax on that income for that year. I think there is an injustice there, but I shall not take up the time of the committee to discuss it any farther. I should like to have it looked into.

In this connection I should like to ask a question which has reference to a similar case. Some individuals in my province were unfortunate enough to invest in bonds of the province of Alberta. A certain government came into power and repudiated them and for years-

Supply-National Revenue
They did not repudiate them.
Wait a minute until I get through.
The hon. member is stupid.

It may be stupid to you, but these are the facts. Certain farmers in my riding-I shall put it in this way for the benefit of the minister-purchased these bonds and they did not draw any interest on them for a number of years. When the province of Alberta reassumed their responsibility for the interest it was all paid in one year. One farmer had an income of $2,240. If he had been paid yearly, without repudiation or delay, as he should have been, he would have received $660 a year. I hope that is clear to my hon. friends across the way. It is absolutely shameful for any government in Canada to adopt such an attitude. They are responsible. Is it not possible to make provision for a case such as that I have outlined? If the interest which had accumulated had been spread over the years when it was due this farmer would not have been liable for taxation.

I am sure the hon. member would like to be set right. In the first place, I think he is wrong in asserting that the interest was not paid. The interest was tendered and it was there for the bond holder who wished to take it.

speechtext: Yes; it is in the same form as the earlier appropriation bill.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

I wish to say a few words in connection with the payment of subsidies on oats and barley. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture has left the chamber, but I am sure the acting leader of the government will relay to him what I have to say and the advice I have to give. My information from the province of British Columbia today is that the farmer gains very little by the subsidy which has been granted on oats and barley because the feed companies in British Columbia, working under what I honestly believe to be a monopoly, have raised their prices to such an extent. As a result, the egg producers will have to produce eggs at a loss unless some action is taken by this government to increase the subsidies, either through the Department of Agriculture or under the omnibus bill.

Carried.

Royal Assent

No, it is not carried yet. I supported the government on the omnibus bill the other day, but on Monday I am going to say something about the control bill. If there is to be a control bill it must be made to work; otherwise it should be withdrawn entirely. I want to make sure this matter is brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. The subsidies have been of little benefit to the egg producers of British Columbia; and unless some action is taken, I definitely intend to deal with the matter under the control measure.
I should like to support what has been said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I have received letters from my part of the country expressing the same view.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
Schedule agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: It can be taken to be six o'clock now, so I leave the chair, and the house will resume its sittings at eight-thirty o'clock this evening. Since the house will have to go to the senate for royal assent, I would ask that there 'be at least twenty members in order to have a quorum.
May I suggest to the government that they protect us in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will do our best.

I will pair with you right now.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at 8.30 p.m.

I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following communication:
Ottawa, March 28, 1917.
Sir:	I have the honour to inform you that
the Hon. Patrick Kerwin, acting as deputy of His Excellency the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate chamber this day at 8.30 p.m., for the purpose of giving the royal assent to certain hills.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
F. L. C. Pereira,
Assistant Secretary to the Governor General
A message was delivered by Major C. R. Lamoureux, D.S.O., Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, His Honour, the deputy of His Excellency the Governor General, desires the immediate attendance of this honourable house in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, the house went up to the Senate.
And having returned.
